key_bets: Heavy ion linear induction accelerator (LIA) driver achieves 30-40% wall-plug efficiency, a structural advantage over laser ICF (1-15%) that reduces required target gain to ~50-70 and recirculating power to ~15%

Modular induction cell architecture (hundreds of identical cells) enables factory manufacturing cost reduction from scientific-instrument procurement levels, potentially halving driver capital from $1.4B to $0.7B
HYLIFE-II thick FLiBe liquid-jet wall reforms within the 6 Hz cycle time and survives 30-year plant life with no first wall replacement
Direct-drive HIF targets (spherical capsule with lead/gold tamper, aluminum pusher, DT ice layer) can be mass-produced at ~9.5 billion targets over 30 years per chamber at <~$3/target (1990s dollars)
Rep-rated chamber operation at 5-15 Hz is achievable, with target injection accuracy, chamber clearing, and driver reliability supporting >78% plant availability
Tritium breeding self-sufficiency is achieved with LiPb (HIBALL TBR ~1.195) or FLiBe (HYLIFE-II) blankets, with low in-system inventory (0.5 g molten salt + 140 g tube wall)
Ion source and beam transport deliver Bi²⁺ at 10 GeV and 160 mA through a ~3 km linac with commercial-duty-cycle availability
eliminated_costs: No plasma-confining HTS/LTS magnet system — eliminates hundreds of millions of dollars of magnet capital and thousands of km of REBCO tape that dominate tokamak/stellarator costs
No scheduled first-wall/blanket module replacement CAPEX — HYLIFE-II liquid FLiBe wall claims 30-year chamber lifetime with no structural replacement
No final-focus optics damage from X-rays and neutrons — magnetic focusing elements do not absorb light and sit at large stand-off from the chamber, unlike laser ICF optics
Reduced target gain requirement (~50-70 vs. 100-200 for laser ICF) due to high driver efficiency, lowering per-shot physics performance demands
Minimal superconducting magnet cryogenics scale — only modest focusing quadrupoles rather than km-scale plasma-confinement coil cryogenic systems
novel_costs: Heavy ion linear induction accelerator driver capital — ~$1.4B (inflated from HYLIFE-II's $570M in 1990s dollars), the dominant single line item at 40-60% of plant capital (C220104)
Km-scale accelerator tunnel civil works — ~3 km linac infrastructure not captured by tokamak-derived per-MW buildings scaling (CAS21 likely undercosted at $622M)
Continuous cryogenic DT target fabrication at 5-15 Hz (~189 million targets/year; ~9.5 billion over 30 years per chamber) with automated fill-and-freeze and quality control

FLiBe coolant inventory (beryllium + Li-6 enriched lithium) sized for thick 30-50 cm flowing curtains around the chamber — uncharacterized in modern dollars and supply-constrained by Materion beryllium production
Induction cell and beam-transport quadrupole replacement at commercial rep rates — component lifecycle costs uncharacterized for 6+ Hz continuous duty over 30 years

risks.description: All published HIF cost data is 30-40 years old (HIBALL 1985, HYLIFE-II early-1990s) with no modern reanalysis in current dollars; 43% gap between model LCOE ($92/MWh) and inflation-adjusted historical reference ($162/MWh) reflects unresolved re-baselining

No private company pursues HIF commercially as of 2026 — 'Intensity Energy' cannot be verified in FIA 2025 survey or any public database; no developer exists to provide design choices or commercial performance targets
Plant availability is the dominant LCOE lever (elasticity -0.96); a 10-point shortfall from 80% base adds ~$9/MWh, and no HYLIFE-II/HIBALL availability analysis exists to bound the 70-90% range

Target fabrication cost at 5-15 Hz commercial volume is uncharacterized — no bottom-up cost analysis exists for ~189M cryogenic DT targets/year, and Goodin et al. (2004) <$3/target criterion is unvalidated for HIF geometry

Driver capital cost uncertainty is the single largest LCOE uncertainty — HYLIFE-II's $570M is the only bottom-up estimate; modular-manufacturing learning curve is unquantified; scenario range $0.7B-$2.5B drives LCOE from $79 to $114/MWh
Ion source and injector at commercial duty cycle are TRL 2-3 — no Bi²⁺/Cs⁺ source at 160 mA and 10+ Hz has been demonstrated; LBNL HIF program ended without building a driver-scale injector

Rep-rated chamber operation at 5-15 Hz (FLiBe jet reformation within ~100-200 ms, chamber clearing of activation debris, target injection accuracy) has no experimental demonstration — HYLIFE-II analysis is analytical only

Li-6 supply chain is a structural gating constraint — no active production facility exists worldwide; 2019 price 53 k€/kg vs. 1 k€/kg historical; ~52 t inventory per 2 GW plant implies €2.5-3B inventory cost; ~20-year lead time to establish capacity
Regulatory pathway and cost are undefined — no HIF licensing engagement exists; Stewart & Shirvan 2.2× construction cost multiplier applies as conservative upper bound for D-T IFE plant

Framework modeling limitations: eta_pin wiring is inverted for IFE (+0.148 elasticity), plasma_t is a framework artifact with no HIF meaning, and CAS21 buildings scaling is tokamak-derived — model LCOE is a probable lower bound
Final focus superconducting quadrupole lifetime under cumulative neutron exposure at 10-15 Hz over 30 years is uncharacterized — no irradiation database exists for HIF final-focus geometry
FLiBe coolant inventory cost is sparse across all IFE sources (only 1994-dollar HYLIFE-II estimates); beryllium supply is dominated by Materion Corp. (USA), global production ~300 tonnes/year

Tritium extraction from FLiBe or LiPb at commercial plant throughput is unvalidated — MSRE achieved 99.7% extraction but at far lower throughput; permeation barriers for FLiBe-facing heat exchangers are missing at scale
Startup tritium procurement (~1 kg at >$35,000/g) and CANDU production decline are shared D-T constraints that limit near-term commercial deployment
sCO₂ Brayton or other advanced power conversion cycles have not been evaluated for HIF — all studies baseline on 1990s-era steam Rankine at ~33-38% thermal efficiency
